tldr: To achieve compliant whole-body disturbance adaptation—including the lower body—on 70 kg-class heavy humanoids, this work proposes a two-stage pipeline where reinforcement learning is guided by analytical impedance targets, and coarse external force estimates are precisely corrected via a residual policy.
hero_caption: The two-stage training pipeline of CompliantWBC. In Stage 1, a base policy and a force encoder are co-trained based on virtual targets generated from an analytical model. In Stage 2, with the base frozen, a bounded residual policy directly edits the impedance equilibrium.
overview:
Humanoids that collaborate with humans require compliance to smoothly yield to external forces. In heavy platforms exceeding 70 kg that handle heavy payloads, preventing falls depends not just on end-effector or upper-body compliance, but on whole-body compliance including the lower body—such as pelvis bracing and hip weight shifting.

However, conventional classical model-based controllers (such as quadratic programming) suffer from brittle contact mode transitions and heavy computational overhead. On the other hand, most recent reinforcement learning approaches restrict compliance to the end-effector or upper body, leaving the problem of learning to absorb external forces across arbitrary whole-body contact sites—especially with lower-body engagement—largely unaddressed.

To bridge this gap, this work introduces CompliantWBC. First, an analytical impedance model is formulated for arbitrary whole-body links, and its target trajectory is used as a reward to guide the base policy via imitation. Furthermore, a variational force encoder estimates external wrenches from joint position and torque histories, and a two-stage training pipeline is developed where a bounded residual policy directly corrects estimation errors on the impedance equilibrium. Additionally, a Phong-weighted sampling method is introduced to effectively apply payload disturbances to the lower body.

In simulation evaluations, CompliantWBC keeps the deviation from analytical ideal responses to just 2.58 cm and significantly alleviates joint torque saturation compared to stiff tracking baselines. Furthermore, deployed on a real 70 kg-class humanoid, it reliably executes five whole-body contact tasks requiring coordinated full-body motion, including whiteboard wiping and collaborative 100 N heavy payload transport.
contributions: Formulated an analytical multi-site whole-body impedance reference controller integrating centroidal momentum balance and arbitrary-link Cartesian impedance to serve as an RL reward.

Constructed a two-stage residual learning framework comprising a force encoder that coarsely estimates external forces from proprioception and a residual policy that bounds corrections within 5 cm directly on the impedance equilibrium.
Proposed a Phong-weighted force-origin sampler that biases load directions downward and decouples horizontal and vertical degrees of freedom, naturally inducing lower-body compliant yielding.
Demonstrated sensorless success across real-world tasks requiring lower-body coordination, such as 100 N payload transport and board wiping, on a real 70 kg-class humanoid.

sections.heading: Why Do Heavy Humanoids Need Whole-Body Compliance Including the Lower Body?
sections.summary: For heavy humanoids to perform heavy-duty tasks, compliant force control that engages the pelvis, hips, and lower body is essential alongside the end-effectors. This work proposes CompliantWBC, a novel whole-body compliance learning framework that overcomes both the brittleness of model-based control and the narrow scope of recent RL methods.
sections.details:
Imagine a humanoid pulling a heavy cart or leaning against a wall while carrying a load. In these scenarios, soft upper-body springs are not enough; the robot must slide its pelvis and redistribute support forces across both legs, yielding to forces with its entire body.

Solving such motions using classical analytical task-space control requires highly accurate dynamic models and quadratic programming (QP) solvers to compute joint torques. However, on 70 kg-class heavy humanoids, slight inaccuracies in contact mode detection often cause control to break down.

Conversely, recent deep reinforcement learning (RL) methods are robust to modeling errors, but most restrict compliance to the end-effectors or upper body. Making the lower body compliant easily disrupts walking balance, and there has been no disturbance curriculum to systematically train whole-body yielding. Moreover, real robots lack whole-body force-torque sensors, requiring external forces to be estimated purely through joint motion (proprioception).

CompliantWBC tackles these challenges at once. Instead of solving an analytical impedance model via QP on the real robot, it uses the analytical targets as an RL reward. By pairing an external force estimator with a bounded residual policy, the robot achieves smooth whole-body contact compliance—including lower-body engagement—using only simple joint PD control during real-world deployment.

sections.heading: Classical Impedance Control and RL Approaches: Where We Stand
sections.summary: Humanoid compliance control has progressed from classical analytical methods to recent learning-based paradigms. However, guaranteeing physically bounded compliance across arbitrary whole-body contact sites, including the lower body, remained an open challenge.
sections.details:
### Humanoid Compliance Control
Impedance and admittance control, which emulate virtual mass-spring-damper dynamics, are standard techniques for maintaining safe contact forces between a robot and its environment. Classical task-space methods offer formal stability guarantees, but they struggle with contact mode identification, and handling time-varying stiffness easily compromises passivity.

To mitigate these issues, recent research has turned to reinforcement learning to acquire compliant behaviors. However, prior work has predominantly focused on end-effector stiffness or upper-body springs, largely neglecting lower-body bracing and compliant yielding, which are paramount during heavy payload transport and support tasks.

### Residual Policies and Latent Force Estimation
Residual reinforcement learning, which augments classical controller outputs with neural network corrections, has also been widely studied. Prior works often add offsets directly to motor commands or target joint angles, making it difficult to establish physical upper bounds on resulting contact forces.

Furthermore, while methods estimating external wrenches (forces and torques) from joint motion histories exist, estimates inevitably retain noise and bias. CompliantWBC intentionally avoids demanding excessive estimator precision, letting the encoder focus on capturing coarse directions and magnitudes, while a bounded residual on the impedance equilibrium safely absorbs estimation discrepancies.

sections.heading: An Analytical Reference Model Integrating Arbitrary-Link Impedance
sections.summary: We formulate an impedance target specifying how the robot should deflect when external forces act on arbitrary links across the body. Rather than calculating joint torques directly on hardware, these targets serve as reward anchors guiding the RL agent toward correct compliant behaviors.
sections.details:
To teach whole-body compliance via reinforcement learning, an ideal anchor is required to define how much each link should physically deflect under external loads.

This work extends conventional Cartesian impedance at a single end-effector to define virtual target positions $\boldsymbol{x}_{\ell}(\boldsymbol{f})$ for any controlled link $\ell$ subjected to external force:
$$\boldsymbol{x}_{\ell}(\boldsymbol{f}) = \boldsymbol{x}_{\ell}^{\text{ref}} - \boldsymbol{K}_{\ell}^{-1} \boldsymbol{f}_{\ell}$$
where $\boldsymbol{x}_{\ell}^{\text{ref}}$ is the nominal position in the reference motion, $\boldsymbol{f}_{\ell}$ is the external force transformed into the link frame, and $\boldsymbol{K}_{\ell}$ is an anisotropic stiffness matrix. In essence, the target position shifts proportionally to the applied force like a physical spring.

A key strength of this formulation is its generality. If controlled links are restricted to the upper body, it recovers upper-body spring frameworks (such as GentleHumanoid); if restricted to the end-effectors, it subsumes end-effector disturbance approaches (such as FALCON).

Crucially, this analytical model is never solved online via quadratic programming (QP) on the real platform. Running heavy QP solvers online introduces computational latency and brittle contact mode failures; hence, these virtual targets are utilized solely as reward functions during simulation training.

sections.heading: Two-Stage Learning and Phong-Weighted Disturbance Sampling
sections.summary: We employ a two-stage approach: a force encoder and base policy are co-trained, followed by a bounded residual policy fine-tuning the impedance equilibrium. In addition, a computer graphics-inspired Phong sampler is introduced to efficiently train lower-body downward compliance.
sections.details:
### Pipeline Architecture and Two-Stage Learning
In the real world, accurate force sensor readouts and dynamic models are unavailable. CompliantWBC resolves this through a two-stage training pipeline:

- **Base Policy and Variational Force Encoder (Stage 1)**:
A variational encoder reconstructs the external wrench $\hat{\boldsymbol{f}}_{\text{ext}}$ via a latent variable $\boldsymbol{z}_F$ using proprioceptive inputs such as joint positions, velocities, and torque histories. A gradient barrier is placed between the encoder and policy to block PPO reinforcement learning gradients, preventing RL reward hacking from degrading force representations. The encoder is trained with four objectives: wrench reconstruction loss, contrastive loss identifying disturbance direction and site, an information bottleneck (KL loss), and temporal smoothness loss. The base policy consumes this estimated wrench and is trained using a compliance-fidelity reward that maximizes agreement with analytical targets $\boldsymbol{x}_\ell(\boldsymbol{f})$.

- **Bounded Residual Policy (Stage 2)**:
Because force encoder estimates contain noise and scale errors, the trained base policy and encoder are frozen, and a lightweight MLP residual policy is layered on top. The residual policy outputs an impedance equilibrium offset $\Delta\boldsymbol{x}_\ell$ strictly bounded to $\le 5$ cm. Since stiffness $\boldsymbol{K}_\ell$ is fixed, this correction exerts a well-defined, physically bounded influence on the robot.

### Phong-Weighted Force Sampling and Axis-Decoupled Anchor
To induce lower-body compliance, appropriate disturbances must be applied to the robot's pelvis in simulation. However, isotropic spherical disturbances fail to sufficiently capture downward gravitational loads like carrying payloads.

To address this, we introduce a sampler inspired by the Phong reflection model from computer graphics. Disturbance force origins are sampled within a 0.5 m sphere around the pelvis from a probability distribution concentrated downward along $-\hat{\boldsymbol{e}}_z$, ensuring the robot frequently experiences downward loading.

Furthermore, an axis-decoupled pelvis anchor is introduced. If force origins rigidly track the pelvis, loads autonomously chase the robot during walking. Conversely, anchoring them purely in the world frame causes forces to grow unboundedly as the robot walks away. By tracking the robot horizontally while pinning only the vertical axis to a reference height $h^*$, natural compliant sinking of the legs and hips is induced.

sections.heading: Extensive Validation in Simulation and on a 70 kg Humanoid
sections.summary: In simulation, CompliantWBC achieved the highest compliance fidelity and drastically reduced joint torque saturation compared to stiff tracking and upper-body baselines. On hardware, it completed five contact-rich tasks, including board wiping and 100 N payload transport.
sections.details:
### Metrics and Baselines
In simulation, evaluations were performed over 100 rollouts against the stiff tracking baseline TWIST2, the upper-body compliant GentleHumanoid, and ablation variants of our approach (w/o pelvis sampling, w/o residual). Metrics included task success rate $S$, free-space tracking error $E_{\rm cmd}^{\rm free}$, torque saturation ratio $\rho_\tau$ (percentage of time torques exceeded 90% of maximum limits), lower-body torque contribution ratio $R_{\rm LB}$, and compliance fidelity $E_{\rm imp}$ measuring geometric deviation from analytical targets.

### Simulation Results
The stiff baseline TWIST2 aggressively resisted disturbances, leading to severe torque saturation and a success rate of only 59%. GentleHumanoid achieved a 91% success rate by yielding with its upper body, but its lower-body engagement ratio $R_{\rm LB}$ remained low at 0.14.

In contrast, our proposed method (Ours full) achieved the highest success rate while suppressing torque saturation $\rho_\tau$ to a minimal $0.93 \times 10^{-2}$ and attaining the highest lower-body contribution of 0.28. Its compliance fidelity $E_{\rm imp}$ reached 2.58 cm, substantially outperforming all other methods ($\ge 3.81$ cm).

### Force Estimation and the Role of Residual Policy
Analyzing force encoder outputs revealed that directional error (angular deviation from ground truth) decreased as load increased, reaching a median error of 19 degrees above 100 N. However, magnitude estimates exhibited systematic monotonic scale biases—meaning direction was accurate, but distance was distorted. The residual policy effectively absorbed this axial discrepancy with equilibrium corrections under 5 cm, bridging 90% of the performance gap to an oracle providing ground-truth simulation wrenches.

### Hardware Experiments (70 kg-Class Humanoid)
Five force-aware tasks were evaluated on the real platform. The robot maintained gait stability under dynamic disturbances while walking. In a 100 N metal bar handover and transport task, it absorbed loads at the wrists, redistributed forces across the pelvis and hips, and transitioned into a stable walk. In whiteboard wiping under heavy pushing, the robot coordinated whole-body posture by leaning its torso back to keep its center of mass safely within the support polygon.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Future Outlook
sections.summary: CompliantWBC blends the precision of analytical impedance control with the robustness of reinforcement learning, enabling whole-body compliance that engages the lower body. This provides an important stepping stone for heavy humanoids operating safely in human environments.
sections.details:
This paper presented CompliantWBC, a whole-body compliance control framework designed for heavy humanoids.

The core of the framework lies in translating an analytical multi-site impedance controller into an RL reward signal rather than solving it online, alongside a two-stage architecture where bounded residual targets safely correct coarse variational force estimates derived from joint proprioception.

Extensive experiments in simulation and on a real 70 kg humanoid proved that the approach significantly outperforms rigid tracking and upper-body-only compliance. Actively engaging lower-body force distribution and postural adaptation represents a critical milestone toward practical high-payload humanoid deployment.

takeaways: Using analytical controllers as RL fidelity rewards rather than solving them via online QP eliminates solver computational overhead and contact-mode switching brittleness.

Without whole-body force sensors, combining coarse force estimation (prioritizing directional accuracy) with bounded impedance equilibrium residuals closely matches performance achieved with ground-truth external wrenches.
Inducing lower-body compliance requires curriculum design that biases disturbances downward (via Phong sampling) and decouples anchor degrees of freedom to naturally encourage leg yielding.
limitations: The disturbance curriculum assumes standing or flat-ground locomotion; extensions to lower-body compliance across irregular terrains or stairs remain unverified.
Impedance stiffness matrices (K) are kept fixed throughout training, without mechanisms to adapt stiffness parameters online based on tasks or environmental contact.
Training the force encoder requires ground-truth contact wrench labels in simulation, which may lead to estimation degradation if significant Sim-to-Real contact dynamic gaps exist.
